subject_line: Notes and fragments in Everybody Is a Bridge
email_body:
Dear Anton,

The subtitle of Everybody Is a Bridge, "poems, prose-poems, notes & fragments", caught my attention, as did the fact that the Botsotso collection was launched with music from African Melodic Remedies. It suggests a book meant to be heard as much as read, which feels close to your work as a playwright.

I would like to ask how you decide when a fragment is finished, and whether life in Makhanda, between theatre, teaching and the page, shapes that choice.

subject_line: A marriage as allegory in The Comrade's Wife
email_body:
Dear Barbara,

In the Sunday Times piece on the 2025 shortlist, you described the marriage in The Comrade's Wife as an allegory for the state of the nation, prompted by the Zondo Commission. I was also struck by the LitNet observation that the novel opens and closes with the same paragraph.

I would love to ask about that circular frame: did you know the ending before you wrote the opening, and how did you keep Anita's private story from being swallowed by the political one?

subject_line: From ice-cream headache to editing Kgositsile
email_body:
Dear Phillippa,

I have been reading about your path from ice-cream headache in my bone (2017) to co-editing The Poems of Keorapetse Kgositsile 1969-2018, and noticed you were among the poets at Poetry Africa 2025 in Durban. Moving between your own voice and the careful shaping of another poet's life's work seems like a rare double vantage point.

I would like to ask what spending so long inside Kgositsile's poems taught you about your own, and how that shows up in your teaching at Wits.

Dear Stacy,

The Breathers, the long poem you wrote with Daniel Borzutzky for the Chimurenganyana series, seems to grow out of the "breathing machines" work you have been doing with Neo Muyanga and others. It also sits interestingly beside An Archaeology of Holes, whose stories swing between fantasy and raw realism.

I would like to ask how a poem written by two people actually gets written, line by line, and whether breath has become a kind of form for you rather than only a subject.

Dear David,

I was interested to read that The Hoof-Printed Rock is a collection of English poems built from Sepedi idioms and proverbs, written by the same hand behind the Sepedi poetry volume Moswarataukamariri, the play Ditlabonnyane and the novel Sejamoledi.

I would like to ask what happens to a Sepedi proverb when it crosses into an English line, what survives and what has to be rebuilt, and how that question now shapes your creative writing teaching at North-West University.

subject_line: Van Asof geen berge ooit hier gewoon het nie na Ontaard
email_body:
Beste Pieter,

Ek het gelees dat jou debuut, Asof geen berge ooit hier gewoon het nie, in 2019 die Ingrid Jonker-prys gewen het en dat Ontaard later met die Eugène Marais-prys en die NIHSS-toekenning vir poësie bekroon is. Die titel Ontaard laat my wonder hoe die ekokritiek en dekolonialiteit in jou werk, in die gedigte self leef.

My vraag sou wees: wat het tussen die twee bundels verander in hoe jy na landskap en taal kyk?

The Author Ledger is 'n onafhanklike projek wat kort skrywersportrette publiseer. Die portret word ontwikkel aan die hand van 'n paar skriftelike vrae wat jy op jou eie tyd kan beantwoord, en die volledige teks word voor publikasie aan jou gestuur om na te gaan.

Sou jy belangstel om deel te neem?

Vriendelike groete,
The Author Ledger

subject_line: Die Getuienis tussen roman en rolprent
email_body:
Beste Francois,

Ek het gelees dat jou roman Die Getuienis 'n kykNET-Rapport-filmprys gewen het, en dat jy saam met Henning Pieterse die MA in Kreatiewe Skryfkuns aan die Universiteit van die Vrystaat begelei, waar studente se manuskripte al as gepubliseerde boeke verskyn het.

Ek sou graag wou vra hoe dit voel om 'n verhaal as film te sien leef, en of jou eie skryfwerk verander het sedert jy daagliks ander skrywers se manuskripte help vorm.

subject_line: From The Mechanics of Yenagoa to Saskatoon
email_body:
Dear Michael,

Going from The Mechanics of Yenagoa to Leave My Bones in Saskatoon, your titles alone trace a long journey, from the Niger Delta to the Canadian prairie, with novels like Don't Die on Wednesday and Rain Can Never Know along the way.

I would like to ask how writing about Saskatoon has changed the way you see Yenagoa, and whether the new book feels like a departure or a continuation of the Nigerian stories that came before it.

subject_line: Night Transit after In a Free State: A Music
email_body:
Dear Peter,

I noticed that In a Free State: A Music came out from Uhlanga Press in 2018, the same year Uhlanga reissued Foundling's Island, and that Night Transit followed with a launch at Exclusive Books, Cavendish Square, in 2023. The subtitle "A Music" made me curious about how you think of a collection as a whole.

I would like to ask whether Night Transit was conceived as a single movement in the same way, and what the journey in its title means to you.
